items.prompt: Orders polls Shipping once a second, asking 'is order #4471 shipped yet?' What is the actual cost of this pattern, compared to Shipping simply announcing the shipment once when it happens?
choices: There is no real cost — polling once a second is negligible
Load scales with (number of askers × poll rate), almost entirely wasted, and the reaction is still delayed by up to one poll interval
Polling is slower to write than an event-based alternative, but cheaper to run
Polling only costs more if the order actually ships
items.explanation: Most polls find nothing new — the cost scales with how many services ask and how often, not with how often the real event happens. And even when it does happen, the asker still waits up to one poll interval to notice, which an announcement-based approach doesn't.
items.reference:
🔁 Polling: cost scales with (askers × poll rate)
📣 Event-driven: cost scales with real events

Why: a poll that finds nothing new is pure waste — the questioner pays for the answer whether or not anything changed.

items.prompt: A team decides their 1-second poll is too slow, so they change it to poll every 100ms instead. What actually improves, and what gets worse?
choices: Both delay and load improve
Delay shrinks, but load goes up roughly 10x for the same number of real events — the root problem (asking on a timer instead of being told) isn't fixed, just tuned
Neither changes — poll frequency doesn't affect load
Load improves but delay gets worse
items.explanation: Tightening the poll interval trades more load for less delay, but never gets you to zero delay or zero waste — it's still asking blindly on a timer. An event-driven approach removes the trade-off entirely: no delay from waiting for the next poll, and no wasted asks.
items.reference:
🔁 Polling: cost scales with (askers × poll rate)
📣 Event-driven: cost scales with real events

Why: a poll that finds nothing new is pure waste — the questioner pays for the answer whether or not anything changed.

items.prompt: Three different services (Orders, Notifications, Analytics) each independently poll Shipping for status changes. What's the core problem an event-driven approach removes here that tightening the poll interval cannot?
choices: The fact that three separate consumers, not just one, are each generating their own wasted-ask load against the same producer
The fact that Shipping is written in a different language than the consumers
The fact that polling requires a database
There is no core problem — three pollers is the same cost as one
items.explanation: Each additional poller multiplies the wasted-ask load, independent of poll frequency. Publishing the event once and letting a broker fan it out to however many subscribers exist keeps producer-side cost flat as consumers are added — polling can't do that no matter how the interval is tuned.
items.reference:
🔁 Polling: cost scales with (askers × poll rate)
📣 Event-driven: cost scales with real events

Why: a poll that finds nothing new is pure waste — the questioner pays for the answer whether or not anything changed.

items.prompt: In event-driven architecture, what does a producer typically know about its consumers?
choices: The exact address and current status of every consumer, so it can call each one directly
Nothing — it publishes a fact about what happened and doesn't know or care who's listening
Only how many consumers exist, not their identities
Producers and consumers must be deployed together to work at all
items.explanation: A producer in event-driven architecture publishes facts ('OrderShipped') without any reference to who consumes them. That's what lets consumers be added or removed later without ever touching the producer's code.
items.reference:
📦 Producer publishes a fact, once
❓ Producer has zero knowledge of who's listening

Why: not knowing the consumers is the whole point — it's what lets consumers change without ever touching the producer.

items.prompt: Which of these is the best one-sentence description of event-driven architecture?
choices: Services call each other synchronously, but over HTTP instead of in-process function calls
Services publish facts about things that already happened, and any number of other services can react without the publisher knowing they exist
A single central service coordinates every other service's next action
Services share one database so they always see the same current state
items.explanation: The defining trait is the direction and shape of the coupling: a fact gets published once, and whoever cares can subscribe — the publisher never enumerates or depends on its listeners, which is the opposite of a direct call or shared-database coordination.
items.reference:
📦 Producer publishes a fact, once
❓ Producer has zero knowledge of who's listening

Why: not knowing the consumers is the whole point — it's what lets consumers change without ever touching the producer.

items.prompt: What role does the broker play in pub/sub that a direct HTTP call between two services doesn't provide?
choices: It makes the call faster than a direct HTTP request
It tracks who needs the message and redelivers it if a consumer is temporarily down, decoupling the producer from consumer availability
It converts the message into a database row automatically
It removes the need for the consumer to do any processing
items.explanation: A direct call fails (or blocks) the instant the callee is unavailable. A broker sits in between, holding the message until each subscriber is ready to consume it — the producer's own request finishes the moment the broker accepts the message, regardless of consumer health.
items.reference:
📣 Producer publishes to a topic
📥 Broker holds a queue per subscriber
🔌 A down subscriber's messages wait — the producer never notices

Why: the broker, not the producer, is responsible for eventually getting the message to every subscriber.

items.prompt: Notifications is down for five minutes while Shipping publishes an OrderShipped event through a broker. What happens to that event?
choices: It's lost — Notifications will never know that order shipped
Shipping's publish call fails until Notifications comes back
It waits in Notifications' queue on the broker and is delivered once Notifications is back up, without Shipping ever being affected
The broker automatically cancels the shipment
items.explanation: The broker holds a queue per subscriber. A subscriber being temporarily down doesn't lose messages or block the publisher — it just delays that one subscriber's delivery until it's healthy again.
items.reference:
📣 Producer publishes to a topic
📥 Broker holds a queue per subscriber
🔌 A down subscriber's messages wait — the producer never notices

Why: the broker, not the producer, is responsible for eventually getting the message to every subscriber.

items.prompt: A support agent asks 'when did this order move from packed to shipped, and was there a failed delivery attempt in between?' A row like `{ id: 4471, status: 'shipped' }` can't answer that. What can?
choices: Adding a `lastUpdated` timestamp column to the row
An event-sourced log that appends every state-changing fact (OrderPacked, DeliveryAttempted, OrderShipped) instead of overwriting a single row
Polling the row more frequently so changes are caught in time
Nothing — this information is inherently unrecoverable once overwritten
items.explanation: A single overwritten row only ever holds the latest value — every earlier state is gone. An append-only log of every event that happened preserves the full history, so 'what happened and when' is answerable by replaying it.
items.reference:
❌ Overwritten row: only the latest value survives
✅ Append-only log: every fact survives, current state is derived

Why: the log is the source of truth; the 'current row' is just a cached view of it.

items.prompt: In event sourcing, what is the relationship between the event log and the 'current state' of an entity?
choices: They're stored separately with no defined relationship
Current state is derived by replaying (folding) every event for that entity in order — it's a computed view, not the primary data
The event log is deleted once current state is computed, to save space
Current state and the event log must always be edited together, in the same transaction, to stay valid
items.explanation: Event sourcing treats the append-only log as the source of truth and current state as a derived value obtained by folding the events — the same operation as reduce() over a list, not a separately maintained piece of data.
items.reference:
❌ Overwritten row: only the latest value survives
✅ Append-only log: every fact survives, current state is derived

Why: the log is the source of truth; the 'current row' is just a cached view of it.

items.prompt: What problem does CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) address?
choices: That a single database can't run on more than one server
That one shared model is often a poor fit for both accepting writes and serving the very different shapes/volumes that reads need
That events need to be encrypted before storage
That producers need to know their consumers
items.explanation: CQRS splits the write side (validating and recording commands) from the read side (serving queries in whatever denormalized shape is fastest for that query), because a model tuned for one is rarely also optimal for the other.
items.reference:
✍️ Write model: accepts commands, appends events
📖 Read model(s): shaped for the query, updated from events

Why: one shared schema fighting between 'fast to write' and 'fast to read' is what CQRS splits apart.

items.prompt: A team has one write model and wants to add a 'shipments by region' dashboard without slowing down every order write. What does CQRS suggest?
choices: Add more columns and indexes to the existing write-side table until the dashboard query is fast enough
Build a separate, denormalized read model shaped exactly for the dashboard query, updated asynchronously as events happen
Poll the write-side table from the dashboard every few seconds
Move the entire write side onto the dashboard's schema
items.explanation: Rather than compromising the write model to also serve reads well, CQRS adds a dedicated read model built specifically for that query's shape, kept up to date by consuming the same events the write side produces.
items.reference:
✍️ Write model: accepts commands, appends events
📖 Read model(s): shaped for the query, updated from events

Why: one shared schema fighting between 'fast to write' and 'fast to read' is what CQRS splits apart.

items.prompt: Do a team have to adopt event sourcing and CQRS together, just because they're often mentioned in the same breath?
choices: Yes — CQRS requires an event-sourced log to function at all
No — you can event-source without CQRS (one model, rebuilt from the log), do CQRS without event sourcing (two databases synced some other way), or do plain pub/sub without either
Yes — pub/sub is a prerequisite for both
No, but only if the team has fewer than three services
items.explanation: The three patterns solve overlapping instances of the same root problem (reacting to change without polling) but are independently adoptable. They compose well together, which is why they're often discussed together, but none strictly requires the others.
items.reference:
📣 Pub/sub — delivery mechanism
📜 Event sourcing — storage model
🔀 CQRS — read/write split

Why: each solves a different instance of the same root problem — reacting to change without polling — and each is adopted based on which problem you actually have.

items.prompt: A service uses a message queue to notify other services of changes, but stores its own current state as ordinary overwritten rows in a normal table (no event log, no CQRS). Is this a valid event-driven setup?
choices: No — event-driven architecture requires event sourcing by definition
Yes — pub/sub (the delivery mechanism) doesn't require event sourcing (a storage choice) or CQRS (a read/write split) to be present
No — this is just polling with extra steps
Yes, but only for services with fewer than 100 rows
items.explanation: Most real message-queue systems work exactly this way: services react to published events but keep an ordinary overwritten-row data store internally. Event sourcing and CQRS are additional, separable choices about how state is stored and queried — not requirements of publishing and subscribing to events.
items.reference:
📣 Pub/sub — delivery mechanism
📜 Event sourcing — storage model
🔀 CQRS — read/write split

Why: each solves a different instance of the same root problem — reacting to change without polling — and each is adopted based on which problem you actually have.

items.prompt: Shipping starts by calling Orders directly over HTTP when a package ships. Then Notifications and Analytics also need to know. What has to change about Shipping's code every time a new consumer is added, if it keeps calling consumers directly?
choices: Nothing — direct calls scale to any number of consumers with no code changes
Shipping has to add a new call (and handle that new call's failures/latency) for every new consumer, making it responsible for knowing who exists
Only the database schema changes, not the code
Consumers have to poll Shipping instead, which fixes the issue
items.explanation: With direct point-to-point calls, the producer must know about and call every consumer, and a slow or failing consumer can now block or fail the producer's own request. A broker removes this: Shipping publishes once, to a topic, with no knowledge of who — or how many — are subscribed.
items.reference:
❌ Direct calls: producer must know every consumer
✅ Broker: producer publishes once, knows nothing

Why: adding a fourth consumer tomorrow requires no change to the producer at all, once a broker is in between.

items.prompt: With a broker in place, Shipping publishes OrderShipped to a topic. What does Shipping's request path actually wait for before it can finish?
choices: Every subscriber to finish processing the event
Only the broker accepting the publish — not any subscriber's processing
The slowest subscriber's response, since it must confirm receipt
Nothing — publish is a fire-and-forget call with no acknowledgment at all
items.explanation: The broker accepting the message is what lets the producer's request finish. Whether Notifications, Analytics, or any other subscriber has processed it yet is decoupled entirely — that's the point of putting a broker between them.
items.reference:
❌ Direct calls: producer must know every consumer
✅ Broker: producer publishes once, knows nothing

Why: adding a fourth consumer tomorrow requires no change to the producer at all, once a broker is in between.

items.prompt: A fourth consumer, Fraud-Check, needs to react to OrderShipped tomorrow. In a pub/sub setup, what does adding it require from Shipping?
choices: Shipping needs a code change and a new deploy to add the new call
Nothing from Shipping — Fraud-Check just subscribes to the existing topic
Shipping needs to double its poll rate
The event schema has to be rewritten from scratch
items.explanation: Because Shipping never enumerated its consumers, a new one subscribing to the same topic requires zero changes on the producer side — this is the direct payoff of the decoupling a broker provides.
items.reference:
❌ Direct calls: producer must know every consumer
✅ Broker: producer publishes once, knows nothing

Why: adding a fourth consumer tomorrow requires no change to the producer at all, once a broker is in between.

items.prompt: Notifications goes down for a deploy right when Shipping publishes OrderShipped. What keeps that event from being lost?
choices: Shipping automatically retries publishing until Notifications comes back
The broker holds the event in Notifications' own queue and delivers it once Notifications is healthy again
Nothing — pub/sub only works if every subscriber is always up
Analytics resends the event to Notifications on its behalf
items.explanation: Each subscriber has its own queue on the broker. A subscriber's downtime only delays that subscriber's own delivery — it doesn't lose the message and doesn't require the producer to do anything differently.
items.reference:
📥 One queue per subscriber
⏸️ A down subscriber's queue simply waits

Why: per-subscriber queues mean one consumer's outage never touches another consumer's delivery or the producer's own request.

items.prompt: Analytics is healthy but Notifications is down. Does Analytics' delivery of the same OrderShipped event get delayed by Notifications' outage?
choices: Yes — all subscribers share one queue, so a stuck subscriber blocks everyone
No — each subscriber has its own independent queue, so Analytics keeps receiving events on schedule regardless of Notifications' state
Yes, but only if they're subscribed to the same topic name
It depends on which subscriber subscribed first
items.explanation: Per-subscriber queues mean each consumer's delivery is independent of every other consumer's health. Notifications being down affects only Notifications' own backlog, not Analytics'.
items.reference:
📥 One queue per subscriber
⏸️ A down subscriber's queue simply waits

Why: per-subscriber queues mean one consumer's outage never touches another consumer's delivery or the producer's own request.

items.prompt: An order's event log has OrderPlaced, PaymentReceived, OrderPacked, DeliveryAttempted (failed), OrderShipped. How is 'current state' computed from this?
choices: Only the last event (OrderShipped) is read; earlier events are ignored
Every event is folded, in order, into an accumulator — the same operation as reduce() over a list — so the final state reflects all of them, including the failed attempt
Current state is stored separately and has no defined relationship to the log
The events are averaged together to produce a status
items.explanation: Folding every event in order (not just reading the last one) is what lets derived state capture things a single 'latest status' can't, like the failed delivery attempt that happened along the way.
items.reference:
📜 Events, in order
➡️ reduce() / fold
📌 Current state

Why: two systems that replay the same log always arrive at the same state — that's what makes it trustworthy as a source of truth.

items.prompt: Two different services independently replay the same order's event log from scratch. What should be true of the resulting state, and why does that matter?
choices: They may differ slightly, which is fine since events are approximate
They must be identical, because folding the same ordered sequence of facts is deterministic — this is what makes the log trustworthy as a shared source of truth
They'll only match if both services use the same programming language
State can only be computed once, by the original producer, and can't be independently rebuilt
items.explanation: Determinism is the whole value proposition: replaying the same ordered facts always produces the same result, so any service (or a brand-new one) can independently derive correct current state just from the log.
items.reference:
📜 Events, in order
➡️ reduce() / fold
📌 Current state

Why: two systems that replay the same log always arrive at the same state — that's what makes it trustworthy as a source of truth.

items.prompt: An order aggregate has accumulated 50,000 events over its lifetime. What problem does a snapshot solve here?
choices: It deletes old events to save storage
It caches the folded state at a known point (e.g. event #40,000), so a rebuild only has to replay from there forward instead of from event zero every time
It converts the event log into a CQRS read model automatically
It prevents the log from ever growing past a fixed size
items.explanation: A snapshot is a cached fold result plus how far it got. Rebuilding resumes from the snapshot instead of replaying the full history, which is what keeps rebuild cost bounded as an entity's history grows.
items.reference:
📸 Snapshot = cached state + index it was taken at
⏩ Replay resumes from there, not from event zero

Why: without snapshots, replay cost grows without bound as an entity accumulates history.

items.prompt: Does taking a snapshot change what the source of truth is for an event-sourced entity?
choices: Yes — the snapshot replaces the log as the source of truth
No — the log remains the source of truth; the snapshot is purely a performance optimization for rebuilding state faster
Yes, but only for entities with fewer than 100 events
Snapshots and event sourcing are mutually exclusive techniques
items.explanation: A snapshot never replaces the log — if the snapshot were lost or found to be wrong, the full history is still there to rebuild from. It exists purely to avoid replaying from the beginning every single time.
items.reference:
📸 Snapshot = cached state + index it was taken at
⏩ Replay resumes from there, not from event zero

Why: without snapshots, replay cost grows without bound as an entity accumulates history.

items.prompt: In a CQRS setup, what does the write side (the part accepting a ShipOrder command) know about the dashboards or read models built from its events?
choices: It has to know every read model's schema so it can write to them directly
Nothing — it appends events to the log, and a separate projector subscribes to the stream and builds read models from it
It queries the read models before accepting any command
Read models are computed synchronously inside the same transaction as the write
items.explanation: The write side's only job is validating commands and appending resulting events — it has no knowledge of what read models exist. A projector, subscribing to the event stream independently, is what turns events into query-optimized read models.
items.reference:
✍️ Write side: commands → events, nothing else
🔎 Projector: events → read model, independently

Why: the projector is what turns a stream of facts into a table shaped exactly for a specific query.

items.prompt: A team wants two very differently-shaped read models — 'orders by status' and 'regional shipping dashboard' — from the same event stream. What does CQRS suggest?
choices: Merge both into one shared table so there's only one thing to keep updated
Run two separate projectors, each subscribed to the same event stream, each building its own denormalized table shaped for its own query
Only one read model is allowed per write model
Alternate which read model gets updated on each event
items.explanation: Nothing limits a stream to one projector. Multiple independent projectors can each consume the same events and build whatever shape best serves their own query, without coordinating with each other.
items.reference:
✍️ Write side: commands → events, nothing else
🔎 Projector: events → read model, independently

Why: the projector is what turns a stream of facts into a table shaped exactly for a specific query.

items.prompt: A user submits a ShipOrder command, and the UI immediately re-queries the 'orders by status' read model to show the new status. What might they see?
choices: The updated status, always, instantly — CQRS guarantees reads reflect the write that just happened
Possibly the old status, if the projector hasn't caught up to that event yet — this is the eventual-consistency lag made visible to the reader
An error, since reads and writes can't happen close together
The read model is deleted and rebuilt on every write
items.explanation: The read model is updated asynchronously by the projector after the event is appended — there's no guarantee it has caught up by the time a query runs milliseconds later. Submit-then-immediately-redisplay UIs have to account for this lag explicitly.
items.reference:
✍️ Command accepted → event appended
⏳ Projector catches up (not instant)
📖 Read model reflects it — eventually

Why: a query issued right after a write can run before the projector has caught up — that gap is eventual consistency, not a bug.

items.prompt: A support engineer files a bug: 'the shipping dashboard is missing an order that shipped 200ms ago.' Given how CQRS read models are updated, is this necessarily a bug?
choices: Yes — a correct CQRS system must always show writes instantly
Not necessarily — a brief lag between a write and the projector updating the read model is expected behavior in an eventually-consistent system, not evidence of a defect
Yes, because 200ms exceeds any acceptable delay in any system
No, because dashboards are never expected to be accurate
items.explanation: Some lag between the event being appended and the projector updating the read model is inherent to the pattern. Whether 200ms is acceptable depends on the actual requirement for that read model — it isn't automatically a defect just because it isn't instantaneous.
items.reference:
✍️ Command accepted → event appended
⏳ Projector catches up (not instant)
📖 Read model reflects it — eventually

Why: a query issued right after a write can run before the projector has caught up — that gap is eventual consistency, not a bug.

items.prompt: A broker may redeliver the same event after a timeout, even though it was already processed. Fix countUniqueShipped so a redelivered duplicate (identical orderId, type, and at) is only counted once.

tests.description: a single OrderShipped counts once
a redelivered duplicate of the same event does not double count
tests.expr: expect(countUniqueShipped([{ orderId: 'a', type: 'OrderShipped', at: 1 }, { orderId: 'a', type: 'OrderShipped', at: 1 }])).toBe(1)

tests.description: two genuinely different orders both count
tests.expr: expect(countUniqueShipped([{ orderId: 'a', type: 'OrderShipped', at: 1 }, { orderId: 'b', type: 'OrderShipped', at: 2 }])).toBe(2)

tests.description: non-OrderShipped events are ignored entirely
tests.expr: expect(countUniqueShipped([{ orderId: 'a', type: 'OrderPlaced', at: 1 }, { orderId: 'a', type: 'OrderShipped', at: 2 }])).toBe(1)

items.explanation: Since a broker can't guarantee exactly-once delivery, the consumer has to make processing the same event twice a no-op. Keying a 'seen' set by (orderId, type, at) means a redelivered duplicate is recognized and skipped, while two genuinely distinct events with different keys both count.
items.reference:
🔁 Redelivery — same event, delivered twice
🧮 Fix — track processed keys, skip repeats

Why: at-least-once delivery is the broker's guarantee, not exactly-once — idempotent handling is what makes that safe.

items.prompt: A dashboard projector must not double-count a shipment if the broker redelivers the same event after a processing timeout. Fix countUniqueShipped so redelivered duplicates (same orderId, type, and at) are only counted once.

tests.description: three redeliveries of the same event still count once
tests.expr: expect(countUniqueShipped([{ orderId: 'x', type: 'OrderShipped', at: 5 }, { orderId: 'x', type: 'OrderShipped', at: 5 }, { orderId: 'x', type: 'OrderShipped', at: 5 }])).toBe(1)

tests.description: same orderId but a different timestamp is a genuinely new event
tests.expr: expect(countUniqueShipped([{ orderId: 'x', type: 'OrderShipped', at: 5 }, { orderId: 'x', type: 'OrderShipped', at: 9 }])).toBe(2)

tests.description: an empty list counts zero
mixed duplicates and unique events count correctly
tests.expr: expect(countUniqueShipped([{ orderId: 'a', type: 'OrderShipped', at: 1 }, { orderId: 'b', type: 'OrderShipped', at: 1 }, { orderId: 'a', type: 'OrderShipped', at: 1 }])).toBe(2)

items.explanation: The same order shipping at a different timestamp is a distinct real event (e.g. a second, separate shipment), not a duplicate — so the dedup key must include enough fields to tell 'redelivered' apart from 'genuinely happened again.'
items.reference:
🔁 Redelivery — same event, delivered twice
🧮 Fix — track processed keys, skip repeats

Why: at-least-once delivery is the broker's guarantee, not exactly-once — idempotent handling is what makes that safe.

items.prompt: Fix rebuildStatus so it folds an order's event log, in order, into its final status string, the same way an event-sourced aggregate derives current state from history.

tests.description: a single OrderPlaced event yields 'placed'
the full happy-path sequence ends at 'shipped'
status reflects the most recent event, not the first

items.explanation: Folding over the ordered event list — replacing the accumulator with the status implied by each event as it's processed — reproduces exactly what an event-sourced rebuild does: the final accumulator value is the current state, derived entirely from the log rather than stored separately.
items.reference:
📜 Log — ordered list of facts
➡️ Fold — reduce() over the log
📌 State — the fold's final result

Why: current state is a derived value, not a separately maintained fact — replaying the same log always yields the same state.

items.prompt: An event-sourced order needs its current status derived purely from its log. Fix rebuildStatus so it folds the event array into the correct final status string.

tests.description: a longer sequence still ends at the last event's implied status
an empty event list yields null (no state without history)
the full sequence including shipment ends at 'shipped'

items.explanation: An entity with no events has no derivable state — that's why an empty log yields null rather than some default status. Every other case is answered purely by folding the events that actually happened, in order.
items.reference:
📜 Log — ordered list of facts
➡️ Fold — reduce() over the log
📌 State — the fold's final result

Why: current state is a derived value, not a separately maintained fact — replaying the same log always yields the same state.

items.prompt: A broker only guarantees ordering within the same partition key, not globally. Fix groupByPartitionKey so events for the same orderId stay in their original relative order, grouped by orderId.

tests.description: events for one order are grouped in their original order
tests.expr: expect(groupByPartitionKey([{ orderId: 'a', type: 'OrderPlaced' }, { orderId: 'a', type: 'OrderShipped' }])).toEqual({ a: ['OrderPlaced', 'OrderShipped'] })

tests.description: interleaved events for two orders are correctly separated, each keeping its own relative order
tests.expr: expect(groupByPartitionKey([{ orderId: 'a', type: 'OrderPlaced' }, { orderId: 'b', type: 'OrderPlaced' }, { orderId: 'a', type: 'OrderShipped' }])).toEqual({ a: ['OrderPlaced', 'OrderShipped'], b: ['OrderPlaced'] })

tests.description: an empty input yields an empty object

items.explanation: Appending each event's type to its own orderId's array, in input order, preserves per-key ordering exactly the way a real broker's partition key does — two different orders can interleave in the raw stream and still each read back in the order their own events actually happened.
items.reference:
🔑 Partition key — events with the same key stay ordered
🔀 Across keys — no ordering guarantee

Why: keying by orderId lets different orders parallelize freely while guaranteeing each order's own events arrive in the order they happened.

items.prompt: Parallel workers process events from multiple orders at once, but each order's own events must stay in order. Fix groupByPartitionKey so it groups event types by orderId, preserving each order's relative sequence.

tests.description: three orders interleaved in the raw stream are each grouped correctly
tests.expr: expect(groupByPartitionKey([{ orderId: '1', type: 'OrderPlaced' }, { orderId: '2', type: 'OrderPlaced' }, { orderId: '1', type: 'PaymentReceived' }, { orderId: '3', type: 'OrderPlaced' }, { orderId: '2', type: 'OrderShipped' }])).toEqual({ '1': ['OrderPlaced', 'PaymentReceived'], '2': ['OrderPlaced', 'OrderShipped'], '3': ['OrderPlaced'] })

tests.description: a single order's events remain in their exact sequence
tests.expr: expect(groupByPartitionKey([{ orderId: 'z', type: 'OrderPlaced' }, { orderId: 'z', type: 'PaymentReceived' }, { orderId: 'z', type: 'OrderPacked' }])).toEqual({ z: ['OrderPlaced', 'PaymentReceived', 'OrderPacked'] })

items.explanation: This is exactly what a real broker's partition-key routing achieves at scale: many orders can be processed in parallel across workers, but any single order's events always land on the same worker in the order they were published.
items.reference:
🔑 Partition key — events with the same key stay ordered
🔀 Across keys — no ordering guarantee

Why: keying by orderId lets different orders parallelize freely while guaranteeing each order's own events arrive in the order they happened.

items.prompt: A handler that always throws would retry forever without a cap. Fix deliveryOutcome so it returns 'delivered' if any of the first maxDeliveries attempts succeeds, or 'dead-lettered' otherwise.

tests.description: succeeding on the third of three allowed attempts still delivers
failing on all three allowed attempts dead-letters
succeeding on the very first attempt delivers immediately
a later success beyond maxDeliveries is never reached, so it still dead-letters

items.explanation: Capping retries at maxDeliveries is what stops a permanently-failing (poison) message from retrying forever and blocking every later event on the same partition key — after the cap, it's quarantined to a dead-letter queue for manual investigation instead.
items.reference:
☠️ Poison message — a handler that always fails
🛑 Cap + quarantine — stop retrying, dead-letter it

Why: without a retry cap, one bad event can block every later event behind it on the same partition key forever.

items.prompt: A message that fails every delivery attempt should stop retrying and get quarantined instead of blocking the queue forever. Fix deliveryOutcome to cap retries at maxDeliveries.

tests.description: with maxDeliveries of 1, only the first attempt is allowed to matter
with maxDeliveries of 1, a first-attempt success still delivers
fewer attempts recorded than maxDeliveries still evaluates correctly

items.explanation: The cap applies regardless of how many attempts were actually recorded — a success that happens after the cap is reached (or that never gets the chance to run because the cap was already hit) doesn't count, which is exactly how a real broker's max-delivery-count setting behaves.

items.prompt: Fix sumFromSnapshot so replaying resumes from a snapshot's saved index and running total, instead of always summing from the beginning of the log.

tests.description: with no snapshot, sums every amount from the start
with a snapshot, only sums amounts after atIndex, added to sumSoFar
a snapshot taken at the very end adds nothing further

items.explanation: Slicing the array from the snapshot's saved index and folding onto its saved running total reproduces exactly what a real snapshot-based rebuild does: the cost of the replay is bounded by how much history exists after the snapshot, not the entity's entire lifetime.
items.reference:
📸 Snapshot — cached total + index it stopped at
⏩ Resume — replay only what's newer

Why: replay cost stays bounded by the history since the last snapshot, not the entity's entire lifetime.

items.prompt: An order with a long history should rebuild its running total quickly using a snapshot instead of replaying from scratch. Fix sumFromSnapshot to resume from the snapshot's index and total.

tests.description: an empty amounts array with no snapshot sums to zero
resuming from index 0 with sumSoFar 0 behaves the same as no snapshot
a mid-history snapshot correctly adds only the remaining amounts

items.explanation: A snapshot at index 0 with a running total of 0 is equivalent to having no snapshot at all — the resume logic degrades gracefully to a full replay, which is exactly the behavior a brand-new entity (with no snapshot yet) needs.

items.prompt: Fix shipmentsByCarrier so it builds a CQRS-style read model — counting OrderShipped events per carrier — while never double-counting an orderId that appears more than once (a broker redelivery).

tests.description: two different orders shipped by the same carrier both count
tests.expr: expect(shipmentsByCarrier([{ orderId: '1', type: 'OrderShipped', carrier: 'parcelco' }, { orderId: '2', type: 'OrderShipped', carrier: 'parcelco' }])).toEqual({ parcelco: 2 })

tests.description: a redelivered duplicate of the same order does not double count
tests.expr: expect(shipmentsByCarrier([{ orderId: '1', type: 'OrderShipped', carrier: 'parcelco' }, { orderId: '1', type: 'OrderShipped', carrier: 'parcelco' }])).toEqual({ parcelco: 1 })

tests.description: orders split across two carriers are tallied separately
tests.expr: expect(shipmentsByCarrier([{ orderId: '1', type: 'OrderShipped', carrier: 'parcelco' }, { orderId: '2', type: 'OrderShipped', carrier: 'fastship' }])).toEqual({ parcelco: 1, fastship: 1 })

tests.description: non-OrderShipped events are ignored

items.explanation: A read model built by a projector has to apply the same idempotency discipline as any other consumer — tracking which orderIds have already been counted prevents a broker redelivery from inflating the dashboard's numbers.
items.reference:
🔎 Projector — events → denormalized read model
🧮 Idempotent — dedupe by orderId, not by delivery count

Why: a read model is only as trustworthy as the projector's ability to ignore redelivered duplicates.

items.prompt: The regional shipping dashboard's read model must stay accurate even if the broker redelivers an event. Fix shipmentsByCarrier to count each orderId's shipment at most once, grouped by carrier.

tests.description: an empty event list yields an empty read model
three redeliveries of the same order still count as one shipment
tests.expr: expect(shipmentsByCarrier([{ orderId: '9', type: 'OrderShipped', carrier: 'zipmail' }, { orderId: '9', type: 'OrderShipped', carrier: 'zipmail' }, { orderId: '9', type: 'OrderShipped', carrier: 'zipmail' }])).toEqual({ zipmail: 1 })

tests.description: many orders across two carriers tally correctly
tests.expr: expect(shipmentsByCarrier([{ orderId: 'a', type: 'OrderShipped', carrier: 'parcelco' }, { orderId: 'b', type: 'OrderShipped', carrier: 'parcelco' }, { orderId: 'c', type: 'OrderShipped', carrier: 'zipmail' }])).toEqual({ parcelco: 2, zipmail: 1 })

items.explanation: Tracking seen orderIds independent of how many times an event for that order is delivered is what keeps the aggregate count correct — the read model reflects reality once per real shipment, no matter how the broker's at-least-once delivery behaves underneath it.
items.reference:
🔎 Projector — events → denormalized read model
🧮 Idempotent — dedupe by orderId, not by delivery count

Why: a read model is only as trustworthy as the projector's ability to ignore redelivered duplicates.

items.prompt: A customer must never get two 'it's on the way!' emails for the same shipment. Fix notificationsToSend so it returns only the first OrderShipped event per orderId, ignoring redelivered duplicates and every other event type.

tests.description: a single OrderShipped event triggers one notification
a redelivered duplicate does not trigger a second email
tests.expr: expect(notificationsToSend([{ orderId: '1', type: 'OrderShipped' }, { orderId: '1', type: 'OrderShipped' }])).toEqual([{ orderId: '1', type: 'OrderShipped' }])

tests.description: other event types never trigger a notification
two different orders each get exactly one notification
tests.expr: expect(notificationsToSend([{ orderId: '1', type: 'OrderShipped' }, { orderId: '2', type: 'OrderShipped' }])).toEqual([{ orderId: '1', type: 'OrderShipped' }, { orderId: '2', type: 'OrderShipped' }])

items.explanation: Notifications needs the same idempotency treatment as the projector: track which orderIds have already had their email queued, and skip any later OrderShipped for an orderId already seen — that's what turns 'the broker redelivered it' into a silent no-op instead of a duplicate email.
items.reference:
📧 Side effect — sending an email can't be undone
🧮 Idempotency key — orderId, tracked before sending

Why: unlike an in-memory counter, a sent email is irreversible — idempotency has to be enforced before the side effect happens, not after.

items.prompt: Notifications subscribes to the same event stream as the dashboard projector, but must never send a duplicate email if the broker redelivers OrderShipped. Fix notificationsToSend to dedupe by orderId.

tests.description: an empty event list sends no notifications
a mix of duplicates and other event types only yields the genuine first shipments
tests.expr: expect(notificationsToSend([{ orderId: '1', type: 'OrderPlaced' }, { orderId: '1', type: 'OrderShipped' }, { orderId: '1', type: 'OrderShipped' }, { orderId: '2', type: 'OrderShipped' }])).toEqual([{ orderId: '1', type: 'OrderShipped' }, { orderId: '2', type: 'OrderShipped' }])

tests.description: order of the returned notifications matches the order the first occurrence appeared in
tests.expr: expect(notificationsToSend([{ orderId: 'b', type: 'OrderShipped' }, { orderId: 'a', type: 'OrderShipped' }])).toEqual([{ orderId: 'b', type: 'OrderShipped' }, { orderId: 'a', type: 'OrderShipped' }])

items.explanation: Preserving first-occurrence order while deduping matches how a real at-least-once consumer processes a stream in delivery order — the first genuine OrderShipped for an order wins, and everything after it for that same orderId is recognized as a redelivery.
